title: Managing Attention in Classrooms Is a Social Justice Issue -issue/
author: Mike Hobbiss
summary: Mike Hobbiss presents two striking psychology studies on 'attention cueing' - using a stimulus to draw attention to a specific location - and argues they reframe classroom attention management as a matter of educational equity, not just pedagogical technique. In the first study (Markant & Amso), children's IQ normally correlates positively with memory performance, but when a simple visual cue is added to focus their attention during the task, that correlation almost completely disappears - suggesting some of what looks like an IQ-driven memory gap is actually an attention-allocation gap. The second study (Markant et al., 2016) finds the same pattern with socioeconomic status in 9-month-old infants: cueing attention effectively erases the usual SES-memory correlation. Hobbiss argues this positions attention as an 'intervening variable' that may underlie the apparent effects of both intelligence and environmental disadvantage on learning outcomes, meaning some students who appear to struggle can see their apparent deficits diminish substantially when attention is deliberately and systematically cued. His practical takeaway, distilled into the motto 'never assume attention; cue it,' reframes deliberate, precise attention-cueing from a pedagogical nicety into what he calls a 'core requirement of equitable education' - since failing to cue attention systematically disproportionately disadvantages students already facing cognitive or environmental headwinds.
points: Study 1 (Markant & Amso): the normal positive correlation between children's IQ and memory-task performance 'almost completely disappears' once a simple attention cue is added to the task - suggesting attention allocation, not raw ability, explains much of the gap.

Study 2 (Markant et al., 2016): the well-established correlation between socioeconomic status and memory performance - present even in 9-month-old infants - also disappears once attention is effectively cued during the task.

Hobbiss's theoretical interpretation: attention functions as an 'intervening variable' that may underlie the apparent relationships between both IQ and SES on the one hand, and educational outcomes on the other.

His practical classroom motto distilled from the research: 'never assume attention; cue it' - meaning teachers should not assume students are attending to the right information by default, but should actively and explicitly direct it.

His reframing of the stakes: because cueing attention can diminish or erase the apparent effects of both innate ability and socioeconomic disadvantage on memory, systematic attention management becomes 'a core requirement of equitable education,' not just a pedagogical nuance.
quotes: As we might expect, there was a positive correlation between IQ and performance on the memory test; the higher the IQ the better the memory.
The correlation almost completely disappears. When children are forced by a task to engage more of their attentional resources to the task, IQ no longer has an effect on memory performance.
Remarkably, the effects of SES can be found in even 9-month-old infants.

Some students who appear to struggle with learning might, at least in some circumstances, see their deficits diminish, or even disappear, in environments where we can assist them in focusing their attention effectively.

If a core responsibility of education is giving every student the opportunity to learn as effectively as possible, regardless of their cognitive or environmental circumstances, then 'never assume attention; cue it' becomes less a pedagogical nuance and more a core requirement of equitable education.
Of course, cueing attention in the classroom is an utterly rudimentary and downright obvious part of teaching. That said, do we do it well enough, or systematically enough?
